summary:
In 2012 NASA’s fire record switched satellites. The newer VIIRS sensor sees small fires the older MODIS sensor missed, so when the two records are joined, fire counts jump overnight. In Canada the joined record rises 6.6 times from 2009–11 to 2012–14, while Aqua MODIS, which did not change, rose 1.4 times. Fire managers cannot tell a real change from the sensor switch.

Emberline repairs that break. For each country it learns, from millions of fires seen by both satellites, how likely MODIS was to see a fire of a given strength. It then rebuilds the VIIRS years as the count MODIS would have made. The result is one burning activity calendar from 2003 to 2025 for 171 countries, carried on through 2026 to the present through the NOAA-20 satellite, starting with Canada, Australia, Brazil and the United States.

We tested it on years the model never saw. The 2012 jump disappears in 146 of 171 countries (1 for the raw joined record). Past fire disasters rank where they should: before 2012 their median rank is 2nd of 23 years, against 8th in the raw joined record.

A user picks a country, a one-click area, or draws their own on a map. They get a month-by-year calendar, a verdict on any month (“the highest December in 23 years”), the critical periods of the fire season, this month against the historical median, and CSV, chart and report downloads. Every number shows its typical error and its limits.
details:
https://github.com/modularktech-hash/emberline

Two joins, both fixed
The fire record has been broken twice. In 2012 it switched from MODIS to VIIRS on Suomi-NPP; today the current data comes from VIIRS on NOAA-20. Emberline repairs both joins, each tested on years it never saw, so the calendar runs from 2003 to the present on one scale and keeps working as MODIS retires.

What it does
Emberline is a web app that turns NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots from MODIS and VIIRS into one consistent burning activity calendar for any area of interest.

  • Pick an area: a country, a one-click area (New South Wales, Amazon basin, Sierra Nevada, Pantanal, Central Africa savanna), a box or polygon drawn on the map, or typed latitude and longitude, plus a month range.
  • Read the calendar: years down, months across, 2003 to today (2026 so far as a provisional row, for the countries the site lists), coloured by detections or against a usual month (blue below, orange to red above, colour-blind checked). Raw and harmonized are one click apart, and it opens on the harmonized record.
  • Get a verdict: click any month for a fire report. It gives the rank among 23 years, how many times a usual month it is, the raw count beside it, the typical error for that country, and the years most like it with what came next. A report page has an HTML export and a shareable link.
  • Critical periods: fire season, peak month, years with the highest burning activity, quietest window.
  • This month against the historical median: November 2026 so far, on the harmonized scale for 50 countries. Australia is on pace for about 21,472, against a median of 13,767: 3rd of 24 Novembers, above the median beyond the typical error (±12%).
  • Downloads: calendar CSV, hotspot CSV (individual detections for chosen dates, or grid cells), SVG/PNG charts, JSON, an evidence brief, a citation.
  • Live layer: the last 24 hours and 7 days from NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and MODIS, labelled raw.

How it works

  1. Match. A Suomi-NPP VIIRS fire counts as “seen by Aqua” if Aqua MODIS detected fire on the same day within about 3.5 km. Both pass at about 13:30 local time.
  2. Learn. Per country, the chance that MODIS sees a fire, given its fire radiative power, fitted on 2012–2018. 130 countries have their own curve. 41 with few fires use a shared curve averaged from 61 others. 66 have too little data and are shown raw, labelled uncorrected.
  3. Rebuild. Each VIIRS fire is weighted by that chance and scaled per country, giving an Aqua-MODIS-equivalent count comparable back to 2003.
  4. Test. Scored on 2019–2021, years never used to fit. The fit stops at 2021 because Terra and Aqua drift to later orbits from 2022.
  5. Continue to the present. NOAA-20 is bridged to the record per country, trained April 2018–2021 and tested 2022–2023. All 50 countries tested pass (median monthly miss 7.25%). January 2026 to the latest day is then built from NOAA-20 (standard processing, then near-real-time) through the same fit and bridge, and shown as a provisional 2026 row on the calendar.

Evidence (held-out years 2019–2021, 171 countries)

  • 2012 jump removed: in 146 of 171 countries the harmonized step is within ±25% of unchanged Aqua; raw joined record: 1 of 171.
  • False records: months that beat every earlier year of the same calendar month, 67.2% raw versus 12.0% harmonized; 10% would be chance.
  • Blind seam test: 2012 is the biggest break in 93 of 130 countries raw, 11 harmonized; chance alone gives 9.3.
  • Known fire disasters: 13 events fixed before results were computed. Before 2012 their median rank is 2nd of 23 harmonized, against 8th raw. For recent events the two are close (3.5th against 2.5th), as expected when both records come from VIIRS.
  • Honest benchmark: four corrections on the same 2.57 million held-out cell-months. Median R²: raw VIIRS −16.2, a fire-power cut-off 0.14, a single ratio 0.59, Emberline 0.55. The ratio follows the ups and downs slightly better; Emberline has the smaller monthly error in 141 of 171 countries. Both remove the 2012 jump.
  • Worked example: New South Wales, December 2019: 11,312 harmonized detections, 59 times a usual December, highest of 23.

Limits

  • Harmonized counts estimate what MODIS would have seen; they are not MODIS observations.
  • Typical monthly error is ±31% (median). It is ±48% where fires are fewest and ±22% where most, and ±54% for shared-curve countries against ±26% for their own.
  • A typical error is a median miss, not a confidence interval.
  • Hotspot counts are active fires, not burned area. Nothing is a forecast.
  • Regional results, not a global correction.

Benefits
A fire manager or researcher can compare a season with the years before 2012 on one scale, and see how unusual this month is. Emberline gives a verdict with the evidence and the limits beside it, plus data to take away. The method carries the record forward as MODIS retires.

Tools
Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, h3-js, hyparquet, react-globe.gl and three.js, satellite.js; Python with Polars, NumPy and h3. Static Parquet files over HTTP range requests, with no database. Hosted on Vercel. Open source, MIT.

Reliability. Nothing a visitor sees waits on NASA. The calendar, fire reports, the 2026 row, the proof and the live-fire globe are read from files published with the site, built from NASA FIRMS data in advance. If a NASA service is slow or down, the site shows the last good data with its date, never a blank page or an endless loading screen. A daily job refreshes the live layer and only replaces a file after it passes the data checks; if NASA errors, the previous file stays up. The map falls back to a plain country outline if the map tiles fail. The one live NASA request, downloading individual hotspots for chosen dates, gives up after 75 seconds with a clear message, and the grid-cell hotspot downloads, from the site’s own files, keep working.

TODAY’S SATELLITE, CHECKED TOO. Today’s fire data comes from NOAA-20, a newer satellite with the same VIIRS camera as Suomi-NPP. We tested it against our corrected record on 2022–2023, years held back from the fit: in all 50 countries tested, its monthly counts land within a typical 7% of the record. So for those 50 countries, this month and the 2026 row of the calendar sit on the same corrected scale as 2003. Australia’s November 2026 is on pace for its 3rd highest November in 24 years.
